source.title: How much do language models memorize?
source.authors: J. X. Morris; Chawin Sitawarin; Chuan Guo; Narine Kokhlikyan; G. Suh; Alexander M. Rush; Kamalika Chaudhuri; Saeed Mahloujifar

record.tranche_reason: The study reports grokking-like delayed generalization while training GPT-style language models on real text, extending the phenomenon to a new data setting.
record.gate_note: The relevant result is the reported decrease in evaluation loss after training on larger text datasets. The synthetic random-bitstring experiments are not rows for grokking because the paper states that generalization is not possible there. Membership-inference and extraction results do not measure the claimed delayed-generalization behavior.
record.test_reason: The paper uses the word 'grokking' for a dataset-size double descent, not for delayed generalization over training time. Figure 4 plots final train and test loss against training-set size for 1.7M–19.2M GPT-style models on FineWeb. Test loss improves once dataset size exceeds model capacity. No training-time trajectory shows test performance improving long after train performance saturates, so the result is a related but different construct (sample-wise double descent). It does not bear on V3's 'grokking-like delays'. The paper also varies no initialization scale or weight norm.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, with one qualification. The authors say models memorize until capacity fills, then 'grokking' begins and unintended memorization falls as generalization rises. Their 'grokking' is a dataset-size double-descent threshold, not a training-time delay. The limitations section even attributes grokking to Nakkiran et al. (2019), a double-descent paper. The main stated contributions are a capacity estimate of ~3.6 bits per parameter and a membership-inference scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains GPT-style language models on FineWeb text and tracks evaluation loss across dataset sizes; it does not use small algorithmic tasks or report the train/test accuracy trajectories of the original grokking setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported generalization-onset sample count depends on model parameter count.

fits_no_version.finding: On FineWeb text, test loss across training-set sizes shows double descent. Test loss worsens near the dataset-to-capacity ratio of 1, then drops rapidly once data exceeds model capacity (~3.6 bits/param). Unintended memorization rises, then falls, as generalization increases. The authors label this onset 'grokking'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sample-wise double descent in small language models begins when dataset information content exceeds model memorization capacity; authors relabel this as grokking.

record.problems: The relevant delayed-generalization result is described in aggregate, without per-model onset values or reported uncertainty. The authors state that their findings are specific to their experimental environment and may not generalize to other datasets, architectures, or training setups.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were reported. Synthetic random-bitstring results are excluded because the paper says generalization is not possible in that setting; membership-inference and extraction results do not measure delayed generalization.

untested.parts: No small algorithmic tasks, no accuracy trajectories over training, no delay-versus-training-set-size measure.
No training-time delay is measured on text. No initialization-scale or weight-norm manipulation.
The 125M and 1.5B models are evaluated only for membership inference. No delayed-generalization trajectory.
No weight decay or low-norm bias manipulation and no ungrokking. The capacity threshold is an information-capacity account, not an efficiency/weight-decay account.
No comparison of learned algorithms across runs.
Precision (bf16 vs fp32) is varied only for memorization capacity, not for any delay.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3 supports V3' rests on the paper's terminology, not on a delayed-generalization measurement. Figures 3 and 4 have dataset size or the dataset-to-capacity ratio on the x-axis, not training steps. Figure 5 tracks memorization over steps only for synthetic bitstrings, where no generalization is possible. No uncertainty is reported for the text curves.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test small algorithmic tasks with training and test accuracy trajectories or whether delay grows as the training set shrinks.
No generalizing circuit, Fourier algorithm, gradual circuit formation, or mechanistic progress measure is studied.
The study reports delayed generalization on text, but does not test images or molecules, or whether initialization scale or weight norm switches the effect on or off.

The delayed-generalization result is reported for models up to 19.2M parameters. The larger-model experiments report membership-inference results, not grokking-like generalization during large-model pretraining or fine-tuning.
The study does not test weight decay or another low-norm bias, a critical dataset size predicted by an efficiency account, or ungrokking below that size.
The study does not identify or compare algorithms learned across runs.
The study does not test whether adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point limits cause the delay.

rows.subject: GPT-style transformers (1.7M, 3.6M, 8.0M, and 19.2M parameters; aggregate result)
rows.operation_detail: Train models on FineWeb text datasets of varying sizes and measure train and evaluation loss.

conditions.value: varied; generalization onset reported at approximately 10^5 samples, depending on parameter count

rows.measure: Evaluation loss during training across training-set sizes
rows.value: For larger datasets, evaluation loss begins to decrease only once model capacity is reached; this takes approximately 10^5 samples, depending on parameter count.
rows.note: The paper gives this as an aggregate description of the model-size curves; it does not state a separate generalization-onset value for each model.
rows.check: The measure is end-of-training evaluation loss across training-set sizes (double descent in dataset size), not generalization delayed in training steps after train fit. It cannot show a grokking-like delay. The value '~10^5 samples' is a dataset-size threshold, not a time delay. The section heading calls it double descent.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
